records.content: Tr Tr Pamukkale University PAU Hospitals Issue a Warning: Let Us Take Precautions Against Seasonal Flu 04.11.2026 TR Assoc. Prof. Dr. Suna Seçil Öztürk Deniz, a faculty member of the Department of Infectious Diseases at Pamukkale University (PAU) Hospitals, made a statement about seasonal flu. In her statement, Assoc. Prof. Dr. Suna Seçil Öztürk Deniz, a faculty member of the Department of Infectious Diseases at PAU Hospitals, said: “With colder weather, an increase is being observed in upper respiratory tract infections and seasonal influenza cases. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health recommend annual flu vaccination for high-risk groups, particularly healthcare professionals, as well as people with underlying health conditions, pregnant women, young children and older adults. Vaccination helps protect against influenza, reduce its spread and prevent the development of serious complications that can be life-threatening, particularly in high-risk groups. Seasonal influenza is an acute infection caused by influenza A and B viruses and can be transmitted through the respiratory route. Common symptoms include sudden onset of fever, cough, sore throat, headache, muscle and joint pain, and pronounced fatigue. Although most people recover from the illness within approximately one week, it can be severe in older adults, young children, pregnant women, people with chronic illnesses and those with weakened immune systems. When flu symptoms appear, it is important to rest, drink sufficient fluids and seek support from healthcare professionals when necessary. People in high-risk groups and those experiencing severe symptoms should seek medical attention without delay. Anyone experiencing shortness of breath, chest pain, changes in consciousness or a significant deterioration in their general condition should seek urgent medical assistance. Antiviral treatment may be administered to patients when deemed necessary by a physician; it is important to start this treatment early. Antibiotics are not effective against viruses and are not routinely used to treat influenza. Medications should be used in accordance with a physician’s advice.” “What should we pay attention to in order to protect ourselves against the flu?” Emphasising the importance of people in high-risk groups receiving the seasonal flu vaccine every year in accordance with their physicians’ recommendations, Assoc. Prof. Dr. Suna Seçil Öztürk Deniz continued: “Vaccination of healthcare professionals also helps protect both themselves and the people they care for. Wash your hands regularly with soap and water, and use an appropriate hand sanitiser when necessary. Cover your mouth and nose with a disposable tissue when coughing or sneezing; if no tissue is available, use the inside of your elbow. Avoid spending long periods in crowded and poorly ventilated places, and ventilate crowded indoor spaces frequently. Stay at home as much as possible. When you need to be in the same environment as others, wear a mask and reduce close contact. Get enough sleep, eat a balanced diet and drink sufficient fluids. To protect public and patient health and ensure patient safety, we invite all citizens and healthcare professionals to act responsibly and raise awareness about seasonal influenza, pay attention to hand hygiene as one of the basic methods of protection, follow respiratory hygiene rules such as wearing masks and maintaining physical distance, and receive the recommended vaccinations.” İlgili Haberler Sağlık Statement from PAU Hospitals on World Radiology Day, November 8: Radiology Is Where Scientific Knowledge Touches Human Lives 08.11.2026 Bilimsel “Orange” Solidarity at PAU DSBMYO: LÖSEV Awareness Day Gathering Held 05.11.2026 Sağlık PAU Hospitals Call for Organ Donation: The Greatest Legacy Is One Left for Future Generations, Not the Grave 03.11.2026 Sağlık PAU Hospitals Conduct Training Sessions to Raise Breast Cancer Awareness Across the University 02.11.2026 Sağlık PAU Hospitals Warn: Psoriasis Can Affect Not Only the Skin but Also the Joints 02.11.2026 Sağlık First Procedure Performed Using New Equipment at the PAU Hospitals Stroke Center 23.10.2026 Son Haberler Bu Hafta PAU WEEKLY AGENDA 20 Saat Önce Bilimsel PAU Academicians Conduct Inspections as Part of the RISE Türkiye Project 06.11.2026 Bilimsel “Orange” Solidarity at PAU DSBMYO: LÖSEV Awareness Day Gathering Held 05.11.2026 Bilimsel Scientific Studies by PAU Academician Featured in the University of Murcia Bulletin 05.11.2026 Uluslararası İlişkiler Provincial Directorate of Migration Management’s Mobile Migration Advisory Vehicle Begins Operations at PAU 03.11.2026

records.content: 11°C broken clouds TFL Updates Search for: Search Search LDN Write For Us Login London News Lifestyle Entrepreneurship Fitness & Health Finance Tech Food & Drink Automotive Travel Global Canada approves first mRNA seasonal flu vaccine for over-50s By LDN Editor 06 November 2026 3 minute read Listen to this article Canada has become the first country to authorise an mRNA vaccine against seasonal influenza for adults aged 50 and over, approving Moderna’s mFLUSIVA for the 2026-27 respiratory season. The regulator also authorised mCOFLU, a combined mRNA vaccine against influenza and COVID-19, for the same age group. The decision was announced on 5 November after markets closed. What has been approved Health Canada’s authorisation covers adults aged 50 and above, a group that carries a disproportionate share of influenza hospitalisations and deaths. The approval follows the US Food and Drug Administration’s decision in August to authorise mFLUSIVA for the same age group. Seasonal flu vaccines have been made using chicken eggs or cultured cells for decades. The mRNA platform instead delivers genetic instructions that prompt the body to produce a viral protein, which the immune system then learns to recognise. The advantage claimed for the technology is speed. A conventional vaccine requires a strain to be grown and characterised months in advance, which is why the annual flu vaccine is sometimes a poor match for the virus that circulates. An mRNA vaccine can be updated to a new strain sequence in weeks rather than months. The regulatory bar Approval for a new flu vaccine platform requires evidence of immunogenicity, the ability to provoke an immune response, and of safety in a large population. It also requires evidence that the vaccine protects against strains that are circulating, which is harder to demonstrate when the virus changes each year. Regulators in several countries have been cautious about mRNA flu vaccines because the correlates of protection for influenza are less well established than for COVID-19. An authorisation for adults over 50 is a narrower approval than a universal one, and it will be followed by monitoring of real-world effectiveness during the season. The combined influenza and COVID-19 vaccine is the more commercially significant product, since it would reduce the number of injections in an annual campaign. Combination vaccines have historically been difficult to develop because the immune response to one component can interfere with the other. What it means for patients For most people over 50, the existing egg-based and cell-based vaccines remain effective and widely available. The mRNA products offer an alternative, not a replacement, and their uptake will depend on how they are priced and whether health systems recommend them. The timing of the authorisation means the vaccines are unlikely to be widely used in the current season, since procurement and distribution for the northern hemisphere campaign are largely settled by early autumn. The more realistic impact is in 2027-28 and beyond. Moderna has been under financial pressure as demand for its COVID-19 vaccine has fallen, and it has been cutting costs while trying to establish its respiratory vaccine portfolio. A first-in-world approval for an mRNA flu vaccine gives it a regulatory precedent it can use in other markets. The wider significance Influenza kills hundreds of thousands of people worldwide each year, and vaccine effectiveness varies widely depending on how well the chosen strains match those that circulate. A platform that can be updated quickly and manufactured at scale would reduce that variability. The approval also marks a shift in how regulators treat mRNA technology. What began as an emergency authorisation during a pandemic is now being assessed through the ordinary licensing pathway for a routine seasonal vaccine, which is a test of whether the platform can compete on cost and convenience with established manufacturers. The 2026-2027 flu season got off to an early and strong start in the United States, experts say. Influenza activity is still considered low nationally, but cases are rising quickly in many parts of the country, especially in the West. As of Nov. 5, flu infections are growing or likely growing in 42 states, according to the latest estimates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That’s not unusual, given that flu activity typically ramps up around this time of year. However, this year’s flu season started way ahead of schedule, with infections rising as early as August. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said in its FluView surveillance report for the week ending Oct. 31. So far this season, there have been at least 1,700,000 illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths from the flu in the U.S., per the CDC. H1N1, a type of influenza A virus, is currently fueling the vast majority of cases. That’s a shift from last winter, when influenza A H3N2 subclade K (aka, the “superflu”) was the dominant strain nationwide. What’s more, it appears that the H1N1 strain circulating in the U.S. has picked up a new mutation which may affect its ability to evade pre-existing immunity, experts say. If H1N1 sounds familiar, that’s because it’s the infamous “swine flu” virus that caused a pandemic in 2009. As the mutated H1N1 strain spreads, doctors are urging people to get the 2026-2027 flu vaccine. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu season and how to protect yourself. Why Is Flu Season Starting So Early? No two flu seasons look the same because the timing and severity can vary from year to year. It’s still too early to tell if this flu season will end up being more severe or what role the mutated H1N1 strain might play, the CDC tells TODAY.com in a statement. However, there are multiple indicators that flu activity is already higher than usual for this time of year. Cases started increasing in late August and early September and have been rising steadily since, per the CDC. The percent of flu tests coming back positive was 9.1% during the week ending Oct. 31. Last year during the same time period, the weekly test positivity rate was less than 1%, per the CDC National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System dashboard. Outpatient visits to healthcare providers for flu-like illness hit 2.8% during the week ending Oct. 17, which is higher than the previous two seasons, CDC data show. Hospitalizations and deaths from the flu are also rising. “Cases are still relatively low, so we’re still in the early phases of a flu surge,” Andrew Pekosz, Ph.D., a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. As of Oct. 31, seven states are reporting moderate to high levels of flu activity: California, Florida, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Texas and Washington. It’s unclear why exactly cases are rising earlier than normal. One potential reason is that people may have less pre-existing immunity to the H1N1 strain with a new mutation. “Maybe that’s why people are getting sick sooner,” Dr. Bernard Camins, an infectious disease physician and professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, tells TODAY.com. The H1N1 strain spreading is different from the H3N2 strain that dominated last winter. “Even people who got the flu last year are vulnerable,” says Camins. When H1N1 started ramping up in late August, the updated flu shots had just started rolling out. “The pattern we oftentimes see with early season flu is that the first strain that gets here is the one that escapes immunity the most,” Pekosz adds. Does an early flu season mean a more severe flu season? Not necessarily, experts say. “An earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. It’s too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will pan out, or whether it’ll be milder compared to last year’s season. The U.S. saw a harsh flu season last winter fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K variant, aka the “super flu.” “We still have to see how bad it will be this year, but I think it is just starting earlier,” says Camins. “The only thing predictable about the flu is that it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Natalie Azar, NBC News medical contributor, said on TODAY. What Is the Mutated H1N1 Strain? Influenza viruses mutate constantly, which is why we get an updated flu shot every year. Experts Say Ergonomic Pillows Are the Answer for Better Support Last summer, flu A H3N2 picked up a host of mutations, which led to the emergence the subclade K variant. H1N1 viruses typically change less often than H3N2 viruses, the CDC says. However, this year, H1N1 (pdm09), subclade D.3.1.1, acquired one new mutation, G155E, says Pekosz. The mutation was first identified in September in Seattle, Washington, according in a preprint paper published to bioRxiv. “It is different from last year’s H1N1 virus, and that mutation position (G155E) we know is important for generating protective antibody responses,” Pekosz explains. This means the latest H1N1 strain may be better able to escape immunity because the antibodies people have from previous infection or vaccination may not recognize it as well. “How that (mutation) is going to affect the disease spread and severity is not clear,” says Pekosz. Even if the H1N1 strain circulating does not match the one included in the 2026-2027 flu vaccines, the shot is still expected to provide protection. “A mismatch is not a black-or-white situation. We may have less immunity, not no immunity,” Pekosz adds. Historically, H1N1 has hit young people particularly hard. The new mutation may make children more susceptible, especially if they haven’t been exposed to H1N1 yet, Azar said. “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. H1N1 Flu Symptoms Influenza often hits suddenly and intensely, says Camins. Common symptoms of the flu include: Fever Chills Fatigue Body aches Runny nose Coughing It can be difficult to distinguish the signs of a flu infection from those caused by COVID-19, which is why testing is important, Camins says. If you test positive for influenza, you can seek treatment with antivirals, which can lessen symptom severity and duration. Antivirals are an especially important tool for high-risk groups, including people over the age of 65, children under the age of 5, and immunocompromised individuals. These medications aren’t available over-the-counter, so you’ll need to see a doctor first. “You have to get that prescription fast ... within the first 48 hours after symptom onset, (or else) they don’t work as well,” says Pekosz. If you experience severe flu symptoms, contact your doctor. When to Get the Flu Shot There’s no reason to panic over the mutated H1N1 strain, the experts emphasize, but it is a good reminder to protect yourself. “View (this) as a a sign to go out and get the flu vaccine,” says Pekosz. Getting a flu shot is the most effective way to prevent against severe illness, complications and death from the flu. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available at most pharmacies, doctors’ offices and clinics. The updated shots protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2 and influenza B. There are multiple options available, including standard flu shots, high-dose shots, a nasal mist and the new mRNA flu vaccine. “Even if there’s a mismatched strain, there’s two other strains that the vaccine will provide better protection against,” says Pekosz. Different flu strains can circulate later in the season, so the shot can protect you throughout the winter and early spring. The flu shot is never 100% effective, Camins adds, and you can still get infected if you’ve been vaccinated — but you won’t get nearly as sick or end up in the hospital. Vaccination is especially important if you’re considered high-risk, but everyone can benefit. The best time to get the flu shot is before the end of October, but the vaccine will still provide protection if you get it later in the season, the experts note. “If you haven’t gotten it yet for whatever reason, now’s the time to get vaccinated because the flu season is starting a little bit sooner and you need at least two weeks for the vaccine immunity to (reach) protective levels,” Pekosz adds. If you aren’t sure which flu vaccine you should get, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. records.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ What is the difference between Influenza A and B? | Explaining symptoms, testing, and vaccines 検査室からみる遺伝子と医療|臨床検査・研究・AI Nov 6, 2026 08:10 You were told you tested positive for Influenza A. Or perhaps you have heard a family member say they had Type B. Why is influenza divided into Type A and Type B, even though it is the same illness? Are the symptoms of Type A more severe? Is it true that Type B is less likely to cause a fever? Can you catch Type B after having Type A? I think some people have these questions. In fact, Type A and Type B are different classifications of the virus. However, you cannot determine whether it is Type A or Type B based on symptoms alone. In this article, from the perspective of a clinical laboratory technician working in a university hospital laboratory, I will explain the differences between Influenza A and B, what can be learned from testing, and the relationship with vaccines. Table of Contents 1. Are there types of influenza other than A and B? 2. What is the difference between Type A and Type B? Type A is classified by combinations of "H" and "N" Type B is classified by 'lineage' 3. Is type A more severe? Is type B milder? 4. How are type A and type B distinguished in tests? Even if it is type A positive, it is usually not known whether it is H1N1 or H3N2 Is there a difference in detection sensitivity between A and B? 5. Can I catch type B after having type A? 6. Does the vaccine cover both type A and type B? すべて表示 1. Are there types of influenza other than A and B? Influenza viruses are broadly classified into four types: A, B, C, and D. Among these, it is mainly Type A and Type B that cause the seasonal influenza that spreads almost every year. Type C also infects humans, but it generally only causes mild symptoms and does not cause major seasonal epidemics like Type A or B. Type D is a virus primarily related to animals such as cattle and has not been established as a cause of human influenza disease. When you take a rapid influenza test at a medical institution due to a fever or other symptoms, the reason you get a result of "Type A" or "Type B" is that general tests mainly target these two types. 2. What is the difference between Type A and Type B? Even though they are both influenza viruses, Type A and Type B have different classification mechanisms. Type A is classified by combinations of "H" and "N" Both Influenza A and B have proteins called hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) on their surfaces. HA is involved in the process of the virus binding to cells, and NA is involved in the process of the replicated virus being released from cells. Type A is further classified into "subtypes" based on the types of these proteins. For example, the following names are often heard. A (H1N1) subtype A (H3N2) subtype H1N1 indicates a combination of H1 for HA and N1 for NA. H3N2 follows the same logic. Currently, the main type A viruses circulating seasonally in humans are A (H1N1) pdm09 and A (H3N2). Additionally, type A viruses can infect not only humans but also various animals, such as birds and pigs. If a type A virus with new properties emerges and begins to spread efficiently from person to person, it could lead to a global pandemic. Type B is classified by 'lineage' On the other hand, while type B also has HA and NA, it is not classified into subtypes like H1N1 or H3N2 as type A is. For type B, the following two lineages are primarily known: Victoria lineage Yamagata lineage Of these, regarding the Yamagata lineage, no confirmed detections of naturally circulating viruses have been reported since March 2020. However, it has not been proven that it has completely disappeared. In recent years, the type B virus confirmed to be circulating in humans is the Victoria lineage. 3. Is type A more severe? Is type B milder? 'Type A causes high fever, but type B is relatively mild.' You may have heard something like that. However, it is not the case that type A always leads to severe illness or that type B always results in a mild case. Both type A and type B can cause fever, headache, muscle pain, joint pain, severe fatigue, cough, and sore throat. Also, influenza does not always cause a high fever. In some cases, such as in the elderly, it may not be accompanied by a typical high fever. In children, gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea may be seen, but it is not possible to determine that it is type B based on these symptoms alone. Furthermore, complications such as pneumonia or severe illness can occur with both type A and type B. Type B is sometimes thought of as a mild illness, but this is not necessarily the case. In other words, it is not possible to distinguish between type A and type B based solely on the severity of symptoms or the height of the fever. The possibility of severe illness must be judged by considering not only the virus type but also age, underlying medical conditions, and immune status. 4. How are type A and type B distinguished in tests? From here on, I will explain from the perspective of a laboratory. The rapid influenza antigen tests widely used in medical institutions detect specific proteins of the virus. In general rapid antigen tests, a protein called nucleoprotein (NP) is mainly the target of detection. For type A and type B, by using antibodies corresponding to each virus, it is possible to determine which type of antigen has been detected. Therefore, the test results are displayed as "Type A positive" or "Type B positive". However, there is something you should know here. Even if it is type A positive, it is usually not known whether it is H1N1 or H3N2 Even if it is determined to be "Type A positive" in a general rapid antigen test, that alone does not tell you whether it is H1N1 or H3N2. Similarly, even if it is known to be "Type B positive," standard rapid antigen tests do not distinguish the lineage of type B. To investigate more detailed classifications, genetic testing or similar methods tailored to the purpose are required. Some nucleic acid amplification tests, such as PCR, can determine not only type A or B but also subtypes of type A, such as H1N1 or H3N2. However, not all PCR tests can identify the subtype. The information obtained depends on which genetic region is being tested. Knowing that a test result is "Influenza A" is different from knowing "which subtype of A it is." Is there a difference in detection sensitivity between A and B? There is one more thing you should know when looking at test results. It has been reported that rapid antigen tests tend to have lower detection sensitivity for type B compared to type A. The US CDC also cites this point as a limitation of rapid antigen tests. However, actual detection performance varies depending on the product used and the conditions under which the specimen was collected. It is not necessarily the case that all test kits have the same difference. Also, for both type A and type B, a negative rapid antigen test does not completely rule out infection. Test results must be judged in conjunction with symptoms, the surrounding epidemic situation, and clinical findings. 5. Can I catch type B after having type A? Since type A and type B are different viruses, being infected with type A does not completely prevent infection with type B. Therefore, it is possible to catch both type A and type B in the same epidemic season. Also, even with the same type A, if the subtype or the nature of the virus is different, the immunity gained from previous infections may not work sufficiently. However, just because you have a fever again after having the flu does not necessarily mean you have been infected with a different type. Since other infectious diseases or complications are also possible, it is important to consult a medical institution if symptoms persist or if they improve once and then worsen. 6. Does the vaccine cover both type A and type B? Influenza vaccines are made with both type A and type B in mind. The following three types have been selected for the manufacturing strains of the influenza HA vaccine to be used in Japan for the 2026/27 season. Domestic influenza HA vaccine production strains for the 2026/27 season Type/Subtype/Lineage selected production strains A (H1N1) pdm09 A/Switzerland/6849/2025 A (H3N2) A/Michigan/105/2025 B-type Victoria lineage B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 A combination of three types in total, two A-type strains and one B-type strain, is called a "trivalent vaccine." The "production strains" referred to here are the virus strains used to manufacture the vaccine. Inactivated HA vaccines used in Japan utilize antigens derived from production strains, and do not contain infectious viruses as they are. Previously, quadrivalent vaccines targeting both the Victoria and Yamagata lineages of B-type were also used. However, since no confirmed detections of naturally circulating B-type Yamagata lineage viruses have been reported since March 2020, the composition of the vaccine has been reviewed. However, receiving the vaccine does not completely prevent infection or the onset of Influenza A or B. The effectiveness of the vaccine also varies depending on differences in antigenicity from the viruses circulating that year, as well as the age and immune status of the person vaccinated. Nevertheless, it is one of the important measures for preventing the onset and severity of influenza. Also, the necessity of treatment is not determined solely by the difference between A-type and B-type. Treatment is determined by considering the severity of symptoms, risk of becoming severe, and the time elapsed since onset. 7. Summary Influenza A and B are both viruses that cause seasonal influenza, but their classification mechanisms differ. A-type is divided into subtypes such as H1N1 and H3N2, while B-type has classifications known as the Victoria and Yamagata lineages. On the other hand, because both cause similar symptoms, it is not possible to determine the type based on symptoms alone. Also, while general rapid antigen tests can distinguish between A-type and B-type, they cannot identify the A-type subtype or B-type lineage. What we would like to convey from the laboratory is that there are things that can and cannot be understood from "Type A positive" or "Type B positive" results. By knowing the meaning of the terms written in the test results, perhaps your understanding of influenza will deepen. Seasonal influenza activity continues to rise across much of the US and is higher than normally seen at this time of year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) latest weekly surveillance report. Clinical laboratories reported 9.1% of respiratory specimens testing positive for influenza during the week ending Oct 31. Clinical laboratories tested 51,351 specimens that week, and 4,696 were positive. Cumulative positivity since Oct 4 stands at 6.8% of 233,110 specimens tested. Influenza A accounted for 98.6% of positive clinical lab specimens. Positivity rose nationally and in most regions. It held stable in region 7 and fell in region 9, which CDC says could reflect incomplete reporting. CDC cautioned that an earlier rise in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity. All data are preliminary. H1N1 Predominates in Public Health Lab Data Of the 513 influenza-positive specimens reported by public health laboratories, 502 were influenza A and 11 were influenza B. Among the 388 influenza A viruses that were subtyped, 379 (97.7%) were A(H1N1)pdm09, 7 (1.8%) were A(H3N2), and 2 (0.5%) were A(H5). Since late May, 83.4% of reported influenza A viruses have been A(H1N1)pdm09, most of them in the D.3.1.1 HA subclade. CDC noted that recently circulating D.3.1.1 viruses have split into distinct groups with different genetic changes in their HA genes, and the agency is seeing more genetic diversity among co-circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses than before. The agency said it is too early to know which viruses will predominate or whether there are implications for vaccine effectiveness this season. Among the 688 influenza viruses CDC has genetically characterized since May 24, 486 were A(H1N1)pdm09, 106 were A(H3N2), and 96 were B/Victoria. Of the A(H3N2) viruses, 101 (95.3%) belonged to subclade K. Related: FDA Clears Roche Respiratory Panel with Expanded Pathogen Coverage Vaccine Match and Antiviral Susceptibility CDC’s antigenic testing found most characterized viruses are well recognized by antisera raised against the 2026-2027 Northern Hemisphere vaccine reference viruses: A(H1N1)pdm09: 140 of 147 viruses (95.2%) were well recognized by antisera to the A/Missouri/11/2025-like reference virus. A(H3N2): all 35 viruses were well recognized by antisera to the A/Darwin/1415/2025-like reference virus. B/Victoria: all 33 viruses were well recognized by antisera to the B/Pennsylvania/14/2025-like reference virus. On antiviral susceptibility, 8 of 654 viruses tested (1.2%) showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. All were A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses carrying the NA-I223V and NA-S247N substitutions. No viruses showed reduced inhibition by peramivir or zanamivir, and none showed decreased susceptibility to baloxavir. Related: Blood Test Predicts How Long Vaccine Immunity Will Last Two New H5 Infections in Washington CDC reported two confirmed human infections with avian influenza A(H5) virus, including one death. The Washington State Department of Health reported both cases in adults who worked at commercial dairy cattle farms where highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has been detected in cows. The first patient developed respiratory symptoms during the week ending October 24, went to an emergency department the following week, was hospitalized, and died. The testing pathway involved several laboratories. A specimen collected at the health care facility was presumptive positive for influenza A(H5) at the University of Washington, then confirmed at the Washington State Public Health Laboratory using the CDC influenza A(H5) assay. Additional testing by the University of Washington identified the virus as A(H5N1). The second patient developed conjunctivitis, and the state public health laboratory confirmed influenza A(H5) during the week ending October 31. The specimen has been shipped to CDC for additional testing. Washington has now reported three influenza A(H5) cases in dairy workers. Human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A(H5) has not been identified in the US. Related: Diagnostic Testing Is First Line of Defense Against H5N1 Related: Labcorp Launches H5 Bird Flu Test Hospitalizations, Outpatient Visits, and Deaths Severe disease indicators are also trending upward. Hospitals reported 8,396 patients admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza during the week, a rate of 2.5 per 100,000 population. The cumulative hospitalization rate in FluSurv-NET is 6.0 per 100,000. The highest rate is among adults 65 and older, at 19.8 per 100,000. Among hospitalized patients with subtype information, 99.2% had A(H1N1)pdm09. Outpatient and emergency department measures are rising as well: 2.8% of outpatient visits were for influenza-like illness, up from the previous week but still below the national baseline of 2.9%. 1.7% of emergency department visits carried an influenza discharge diagnosis, also an increase. Two jurisdictions reported high influenza-like illness activity, and five reported moderate activity. Influenza accounted for 0.3% of deaths during the week, a figure that has remained stable week to week but has trended upward over the past 7 weeks. Two pediatric deaths from the 2026-2027 season were reported this week, bringing the season total to three. Three additional deaths from the 2025-2026 season were also reported, bringing that season’s total to 202. CDC’s preliminary in-season assessment classifies severity as low across all age groups, though it may change as activity increases. The agency estimates at least 1.7 million illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations, and 1,400 deaths so far this season. Related: FDA Clears Sekisui Diagnostics Rapid COVID-19 and Flu A&B Combo Test Forecast and Recommendations CDC’s FluSight forecasts predict a likely national increase in both flu hospital admissions and the percentage of emergency department visits due to flu for the week ending November 21. New admissions are projected to range from 6,900 to 30,100, and emergency department visits from 1.6% to 6.7%. CDC continues to recommend annual influenza vaccination for people 6 months and older, and urges those not yet vaccinated this season to get vaccinated now. The agency also notes that prescription antivirals should be started as early as possible, particularly for patients at higher risk for complications. The 2026-2027 flu season got off to an early and strong start in the United States, experts say. Influenza activity is still considered low nationally, but cases are rising quickly in many parts of the country, especially in the West. As of Nov. 5, flu infections are growing or likely growing in 42 states, according to the latest estimates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That’s not unusual, given that flu activity typically ramps up around this time of year. However, this year’s flu season started way ahead of schedule, with infections rising as early as August. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said in its FluView surveillance report for the week ending Oct. 31. So far this season, there have been at least 1,700,000 illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths from the flu in the U.S., per the CDC. H1N1, a type of influenza A virus, is currently fueling the vast majority of cases. That’s a shift from last winter, when influenza A H3N2 subclade K (aka, the “superflu”) was the dominant strain nationwide. What’s more, it appears that the H1N1 strain circulating in the U.S. has picked up a new mutation which may affect its ability to evade pre-existing immunity, experts say. If H1N1 sounds familiar, that’s because it’s the infamous “swine flu” virus that caused a pandemic in 2009. As the mutated H1N1 strain spreads, doctors are urging people to get the 2026-2027 flu vaccine. Here’s what to know about this year’s flu season and how to protect yourself. Why Is Flu Season Starting So Early? No two flu seasons look the same because the timing and severity can vary from year to year. It’s still too early to tell if this flu season will end up being more severe or what role the mutated H1N1 strain might play, the CDC tells TODAY.com in a statement. However, there are multiple indicators that flu activity is already higher than usual for this time of year. Cases started increasing in late August and early September and have been rising steadily since, per the CDC. The percent of flu tests coming back positive was 9.1% during the week ending Oct. 31. Last year during the same time period, the weekly test positivity rate was less than 1%, per the CDC National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System dashboard. Outpatient visits to healthcare providers for flu-like illness hit 2.8% during the week ending Oct. 17, which is higher than the previous two seasons, CDC data show. Hospitalizations and deaths from the flu are also rising. “Cases are still relatively low, so we’re still in the early phases of a flu surge,” Andrew Pekosz, Ph.D., a virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. As of Oct. 31, seven states are reporting moderate to high levels of flu activity: California, Florida, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Texas and Washington. It’s unclear why exactly cases are rising earlier than normal. One potential reason is that people may have less pre-existing immunity to the H1N1 strain with a new mutation. “Maybe that’s why people are getting sick sooner,” Dr. Bernard Camins, an infectious disease physician and professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, tells TODAY.com. The H1N1 strain spreading is different from the H3N2 strain that dominated last winter. “Even people who got the flu last year are vulnerable,” says Camins. When H1N1 started ramping up in late August, the updated flu shots had just started rolling out. “The pattern we oftentimes see with early season flu is that the first strain that gets here is the one that escapes immunity the most,” Pekosz adds. Does an early flu season mean a more severe flu season? Not necessarily, experts say. “An earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. It’s too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will pan out, or whether it’ll be milder compared to last year’s season. The U.S. saw a harsh flu season last winter fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K variant, aka the “super flu.” “We still have to see how bad it will be this year, but I think it is just starting earlier,” says Camins. “The only thing predictable about the flu is that it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Natalie Azar, NBC News medical contributor, said on TODAY. What Is the Mutated H1N1 Strain? Influenza viruses mutate constantly, which is why we get an updated flu shot every year. Last summer, flu A H3N2 picked up a host of mutations, which led to the emergence the subclade K variant. H1N1 viruses typically change less often than H3N2 viruses, the CDC says. However, this year, H1N1 (pdm09), subclade D.3.1.1, acquired one new mutation, G155E, says Pekosz. The mutation was first identified in September in Seattle, Washington, according in a preprint paper published to bioRxiv. “It is different from last year’s H1N1 virus, and that mutation position (G155E) we know is important for generating protective antibody responses,” Pekosz explains. This means the latest H1N1 strain may be better able to escape immunity because the antibodies people have from previous infection or vaccination may not recognize it as well. “How that (mutation) is going to affect the disease spread and severity is not clear,” says Pekosz. Even if the H1N1 strain circulating does not match the one included in the 2026-2027 flu vaccines, the shot is still expected to provide protection. “A mismatch is not a black-or-white situation. We may have less immunity, not no immunity,” Pekosz adds. Historically, H1N1 has hit young people particularly hard. The new mutation may make children more susceptible, especially if they haven’t been exposed to H1N1 yet, Azar said. “It is too early to know what viruses may predominate or to say whether there might be implications on flu vaccine effectiveness this season,” the CDC said in its latest FluView report. H1N1 Flu Symptoms Influenza often hits suddenly and intensely, says Camins. Common symptoms of the flu include: Fever Chills Fatigue Body aches Runny nose Coughing It can be difficult to distinguish the signs of a flu infection from those caused by COVID-19, which is why testing is important, Camins says. If you test positive for influenza, you can seek treatment with antivirals, which can lessen symptom severity and duration. Antivirals are an especially important tool for high-risk groups, including people over the age of 65, children under the age of 5, and immunocompromised individuals. These medications aren’t available over-the-counter, so you’ll need to see a doctor first. “You have to get that prescription fast ... within the first 48 hours after symptom onset, (or else) they don’t work as well,” says Pekosz. If you experience severe flu symptoms, contact your doctor. When to Get the Flu Shot There’s no reason to panic over the mutated H1N1 strain, the experts emphasize, but it is a good reminder to protect yourself. “View (this) as a a sign to go out and get the flu vaccine,” says Pekosz. Getting a flu shot is the most effective way to prevent against severe illness, complications and death from the flu. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available at most pharmacies, doctors’ offices and clinics. The updated shots protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2 and influenza B. There are multiple options available, including standard flu shots, high-dose shots, a nasal mist and the new mRNA flu vaccine. “Even if there’s a mismatched strain, there’s two other strains that the vaccine will provide better protection against,” says Pekosz. Different flu strains can circulate later in the season, so the shot can protect you throughout the winter and early spring. The flu shot is never 100% effective, Camins adds, and you can still get infected if you’ve been vaccinated — but you won’t get nearly as sick or end up in the hospital. Vaccination is especially important if you’re considered high-risk, but everyone can benefit. The best time to get the flu shot is before the end of October, but the vaccine will still provide protection if you get it later in the season, the experts note. “If you haven’t gotten it yet for whatever reason, now’s the time to get vaccinated because the flu season is starting a little bit sooner and you need at least two weeks for the vaccine immunity to (reach) protective levels,” Pekosz adds. If you aren’t sure which flu vaccine you should get, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. Share Add TODAY to Google Caroline Kee Caroline Kee is a health reporter at TODAY based in New York City. records.content: 流感盯上孩子!家长如何科学认识和有效预防? 陇原健康 2026-11-06 20:03发布于甘肃陇原健康官方账号 问AI · 流感疫苗每年更新配方基于何种流行趋势? 每年秋冬季节,儿童流感都会成为家长们关心的焦点。根据国家流感中心最新监测[1],北方阳性率略有上升,南方略有下降。全国流感阳性样本中,甲型占67.6%、乙型占32.4%;甲型中以H3N2为主,H1N1也占一定比例,乙型均为B(Victoria)系。可见甲型H3N2、甲型H1N1和乙型B(Victoria)系流感病毒都在传播,并不是某一种病毒“一家独大” ,且目前监测的流感病毒对常用的两类抗流感药物总体仍保持敏感。家长不用费劲猜到底是哪一种,更重要的是观察孩子症状和精神状态,必要时及时就医。 儿童流感的症状特点 流感通常起病较急,发热、乏力、头痛、肌肉酸痛等全身症状往往比普通感冒更明显。不管是H3N2、H1N1还是乙型流感,孩子都可能出现:发烧、咳嗽、嗓子疼、头疼、浑身没劲、肌肉酸痛等症状。有些孩子感染乙型流感后,还可能出现恶心、呕吐、拉肚子的症状。但要提醒一句:不能因为孩子吐了,就认定是乙流,也不能因为烧得高,就认定是甲流。 该图片疑似使用了AI生成技术,请谨慎甄别 01 0~3岁儿童: 流感的症状不典型,可能表现出食欲不振、呕吐、腹泻、易哭闹、呼吸急促等症状。新生儿可能仅表现为嗜睡、拒奶、呼吸暂停,需要家长格外留意。 02 3~6岁儿童: 多表现为明显的发热、咳嗽和喉咙痛,活动较平时有减少,进入公共场所,与他人保持安全社交距离,勤洗手,戴好口罩。 03 6岁以上儿童: 症状接近成人,可能出现寒战、高热,全身症状(肌肉酸痛、乏力等)较明显。 特别提醒: 如果孩子本身还有哮喘、心脏病、神经系统疾病或免疫功能较弱,更要早点看医生。 怀疑流感,必要时还是要“验一验” 流感季里,孩子突然发烧、浑身没劲、肌肉酸痛,确实要想到流感。但秋冬季呼吸道病毒很多,流感、呼吸道合胞病毒、腺病毒等,有时症状很相似。所以,如果孩子年龄小、症状重、有基础疾病,或者病情越来越重,应及时就医,由医生判断是否需要进行流感抗原、核酸等检查。 需要提醒的是,抗原检测阴性也不能百分之百排除流感。 该图片疑似使用了AI生成技术,请谨慎甄别 何时需要立即就医? 需要提醒家长的是,若儿童出现发热、咳嗽、咽痛等流感症状,同时还有以下情况: 01 精神和神志改变,如反应迟钝、嗜睡、烦躁、惊厥 02 呼吸困难和/或呼吸频率加快 03 严重呕吐、腹泻,出现脱水表现 04 尿量明显减少,四肢末梢冰冷,皮肤颜色差 05 原有基础疾病(如哮喘)明显加重 06 高热持续不退、喂养困难等 治疗抓住“黄金48小时” 记住“1个黄金时间(48小时内)、2类手段(抗病毒药+护理)、3个禁忌(不滥用抗生素、不硬扛、不混搭药)”,就能科学应对流感,守护自己和家人健康! 1 症状出现48小时内是抗病毒治疗的“黄金窗口期”,但不是治疗“截止线”。对于病情较重、持续加重或属于高风险人群的孩子,即使超过48小时,也应及时就医,由医生评估是否需要抗病毒治疗。 2 尽早就医确诊,进行病原学检测 3 遵医嘱使用抗病毒药物,切勿自行用药 4 不滥用抗生素(对病毒无效) 5 不混合使用多种药物 轻症患儿居家护理要点 对于轻症流感患儿可居家隔离,居家期间应当密切关注体温变化,观察咳嗽、咳痰、呼吸困难等症状是否加重,遵医嘱用药。同时还应做到: 保证充足的睡眠,避免劳累; 多喝水,均衡饮食,摄入富含蛋白质、维生素和矿物质的食物; 注意个人卫生,勤洗手,房间保持通风,定时清洁地面; 患儿咳嗽时应用干净的手绢、纸巾或衣袖遮盖口鼻,及时清理污染物; 家庭成员应尽量保持距离、戴口罩,注意防护。 预防是关键 1.疫苗接种 每年的流感病毒都会有些变化,流感疫苗也会根据流行情况进行调整。每年接种流感疫苗是预防流感、降低重症和并发症风险的重要措施。建议在9—10月尽早完成接种,如果错过了这个时间,在整个流感流行季仍然可以接种。 2.养成良好卫生习惯 勤洗手 保持环境清洁和通风 在流感流行季尽量避免去人群聚集场所,避免接触呼吸道感染患者 咳嗽或打喷嚏时,用上臂或纸巾、毛巾等遮住口鼻,随后及时洗手,避免接触眼睛、鼻或口 家庭成员出现流感患者时要尽量避免互相接触,出现流感症状的患儿去医院就诊时,应做好防护(如戴口罩),避免交叉感染 返校提醒 流感患儿平均排毒时间为4~8天,即使在症状出现48小时内接受抗流感病毒治疗,患儿的平均排毒时间仍为3~5天。中位退热时间为2天,这意味着即使孩子退热、流感症状好转,后续仍可能持续排毒约2天。 因此,建议流感患儿体温恢复正常、症状消失48小时后再返校,降低流感校园传播风险。 流感虽然凶猛,但科学应对可有效预防。愿每个孩子都能呼吸顺畅,健康成长,拥抱每一个清新的冬日。 参考文献: [1]中国疾病预防控制中心。2026年第43周第932期中国流感监测周报[EB/OL].2026-10-28.中国疾控中心第43周流感监测周报。 [2]中国疾病预防控制中心.中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027)[EB/OL].(2026-09-02)[2026-11-05].中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027) (来源:兰州大学第一医院) 主办丨甘肃省卫生健康委 编辑制作丨新甘肃·每日甘肃网、省卫生健康宣教中心 审核丨一审 庞传伟、常晓婷 审核丨二审 安 娜、马 菁、白 雪 审核丨三审 杨敬科、陆一鸣

records.content: Diagnostic Technologies Anatomic Pathology Clinical Chemistry Digital Pathology Flow Cytometry Hematology & Serology Immunoassay Mass Spectrometry Microbiology Molecular Diagnostics Point-of-Care Urinalysis & Toxicology Lab Products Biochemicals & Chemical Reagents Information Technology Lab Automation Lab Equipment Lab Safety Labware & Consumables Quality Systems Disease States Allergy & Autoimmune Cancer Cardiovascular Cerebrovascular Dementias & Alzheimer’s Diabetes & Metabolic Diseases Infectious Diseases Kidney Disease Respiratory Disease Sepsis Womens Health Lab Management Accreditation Company News Compliance Proficiency Testing Resource Center Resources Podcasts Webcasts White Papers Videos Comparison Guides Edition Archive Select Page Early Flu Season Activity Climbs as H1N1 Dominates Lab Detections Nov 9, 2026 | Emerging & Zoonotic Diseases, Flu & Respiratory Infections | CDC surveillance data show influenza activity higher than typical for early November, with Washington state public health laboratories confirming two new H5 infections. Seasonal influenza activity continues to rise across much of the US and is higher than normally seen at this time of year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) latest weekly surveillance report. Clinical laboratories reported 9.1% of respiratory specimens testing positive for influenza during the week ending Oct 31. Clinical laboratories tested 51,351 specimens that week, and 4,696 were positive. Cumulative positivity since Oct 4 stands at 6.8% of 233,110 specimens tested. Influenza A accounted for 98.6% of positive clinical lab specimens. Positivity rose nationally and in most regions. It held stable in region 7 and fell in region 9, which CDC says could reflect incomplete reporting. CDC cautioned that an earlier rise in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity. All data are preliminary. H1N1 Predominates in Public Health Lab Data Of the 513 influenza-positive specimens reported by public health laboratories, 502 were influenza A and 11 were influenza B. Among the 388 influenza A viruses that were subtyped, 379 (97.7%) were A(H1N1)pdm09, 7 (1.8%) were A(H3N2), and 2 (0.5%) were A(H5). Since late May, 83.4% of reported influenza A viruses have been A(H1N1)pdm09, most of them in the D.3.1.1 HA subclade. CDC noted that recently circulating D.3.1.1 viruses have split into distinct groups with different genetic changes in their HA genes, and the agency is seeing more genetic diversity among co-circulating A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses than before. The agency said it is too early to know which viruses will predominate or whether there are implications for vaccine effectiveness this season. Among the 688 influenza viruses CDC has genetically characterized since May 24, 486 were A(H1N1)pdm09, 106 were A(H3N2), and 96 were B/Victoria. Of the A(H3N2) viruses, 101 (95.3%) belonged to subclade K. Related: FDA Clears Roche Respiratory Panel with Expanded Pathogen Coverage Vaccine Match and Antiviral Susceptibility CDC’s antigenic testing found most characterized viruses are well recognized by antisera raised against the 2026-2027 Northern Hemisphere vaccine reference viruses: A(H1N1)pdm09: 140 of 147 viruses (95.2%) were well recognized by antisera to the A/Missouri/11/2025-like reference virus. A(H3N2): all 35 viruses were well recognized by antisera to the A/Darwin/1415/2025-like reference virus. B/Victoria: all 33 viruses were well recognized by antisera to the B/Pennsylvania/14/2025-like reference virus. On antiviral susceptibility, 8 of 654 viruses tested (1.2%) showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. All were A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses carrying the NA-I223V and NA-S247N substitutions. No viruses showed reduced inhibition by peramivir or zanamivir, and none showed decreased susceptibility to baloxavir. Related: Blood Test Predicts How Long Vaccine Immunity Will Last Two New H5 Infections in Washington CDC reported two confirmed human infections with avian influenza A(H5) virus, including one death. The Washington State Department of Health reported both cases in adults who worked at commercial dairy cattle farms where highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has been detected in cows. The first patient developed respiratory symptoms during the week ending October 24, went to an emergency department the following week, was hospitalized, and died. The testing pathway involved several laboratories. A specimen collected at the health care facility was presumptive positive for influenza A(H5) at the University of Washington, then confirmed at the Washington State Public Health Laboratory using the CDC influenza A(H5) assay. Additional testing by the University of Washington identified the virus as A(H5N1). The second patient developed conjunctivitis, and the state public health laboratory confirmed influenza A(H5) during the week ending October 31. The specimen has been shipped to CDC for additional testing. Washington has now reported three influenza A(H5) cases in dairy workers. Human-to-human transmission of avian influenza A(H5) has not been identified in the US. Hospitals reported 8,396 patients admitted with laboratory-confirmed influenza during the week, a rate of 2.5 per 100,000 population. The cumulative hospitalization rate in FluSurv-NET is 6.0 per 100,000. The highest rate is among adults 65 and older, at 19.8 per 100,000. Among hospitalized patients with subtype information, 99.2% had A(H1N1)pdm09. Outpatient and emergency department measures are rising as well: 2.8% of outpatient visits were for influenza-like illness, up from the previous week but still below the national baseline of 2.9%. 1.7% of emergency department visits carried an influenza discharge diagnosis, also an increase. Two jurisdictions reported high influenza-like illness activity, and five reported moderate activity. Influenza accounted for 0.3% of deaths during the week, a figure that has remained stable week to week but has trended upward over the past 7 weeks. Two pediatric deaths from the 2026-2027 season were reported this week, bringing the season total to three. Three additional deaths from the 2025-2026 season were also reported, bringing that season’s total to 202. CDC’s preliminary in-season assessment classifies severity as low across all age groups, though it may change as activity increases. The agency estimates at least 1.7 million illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations, and 1,400 deaths so far this season. New admissions are projected to range from 6,900 to 30,100, and emergency department visits from 1.6% to 6.7%. CDC continues to recommend annual influenza vaccination for people 6 months and older, and urges those not yet vaccinated this season to get vaccinated now. The agency also notes that prescription antivirals should be started as early as possible, particularly for patients at higher risk for complications. records.content: Members of a charity organisation disinfect the coffin of a person who died from the H1N1 influenza virus during a funeral service at Yay Way cemetery in Yangon on June 22, 2019. - Three people have died from the H1N1 influenza virus in Yangon and four others have been diagnosed with the virus, the Ministry of Health confirmed on June 19. (Photo by Sai Aung MAIN / AFP) SAI AUNG MAIN/AFP via Getty Images South Korea is recording flu deaths at five times last year's rate, with 21 confirmed influenza fatalities in a single surveillance week and hospitalizations running at nearly triple last year's pace — the clearest sign yet that the country's 2026–27 flu season, which began the second-earliest in recorded Korean history, is not simply arriving ahead of schedule but arriving at a severity that most seasons never reach at all. That figure comes from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency's (KDCA) sentinel surveillance system for the week of October 25–31, 2026 — Week 44 of the epidemiological year — when the agency also recorded 22.8 per 1,000 outpatients nationally as the influenza-like illness (ILI) rate, an 18.8% jump from the prior week. Among school-age children aged 7 to 12, the rate was 60.9 per 1,000 — meaning roughly one in every 16 children in that age group sought care for flu-like symptoms in a single week. Into that surge, Chungbuk Province (North Chungcheong Province) is launching a one-month intensive free flu vaccination campaign for all children in the province starting Monday, November 9. The campaign runs through December 8, though free doses remain available through April 30, 2027. With roughly 40% of Korea's nationally eligible children vaccinated as of late October, the province is targeting the gap directly. Why This Season Is Different Korea's flu seasons do not normally look like this in October. The epidemic alert — formally called the influenza epidemic advisory (유행주의보) — was issued on September 11 , the second-earliest advisory in the history of Korea's sentinel surveillance system, which has been running since 1999. The only earlier alert came during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. The strain driving the current outbreak is influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, the same lineage that caused that 2009 pandemic. After the pandemic ended, that virus did not disappear — it became seasonal, displacing the H1N1 strains that had circulated before 2009 and settling into the annual roster of circulating influenza subtypes. It is now the dominant strain in this season's Korean surveillance data, accounting for the overwhelming majority of positive influenza specimens, and Korean and Japanese surveillance systems have both identified it as the primary circulating subtype this season. China, by contrast, is seeing a mix of H1N1pdm09 and A(H3N2). What makes H1N1pdm09 particularly potent in school-age populations relates to immune history. Older adults — those who were exposed to H1N1 strains that circulated before 1957 — retain partial cross-reactive immunity to the pandemic-lineage virus. Children born after 2009 have no such baseline immunity unless they have been vaccinated or previously infected. The result, visible in the KDCA data, is that school-age children bear the brunt of community transmission when vaccination coverage is low: the 60.9/1,000 ILI rate among 7- to 12-year-olds in Week 44 was the highest of any demographic group, dwarfing rates in adults and even in younger children. The speed of the season's arrival amplified the effect. The national ILI rate had already hit 25.3 per 1,000 outpatients — nearly double the season's epidemic threshold of 12.9 — by Week 36 (August 30–September 5), a point in the calendar year when earlier flu seasons were only beginning to show any activity at all. By Week 39 (September 20–26), the rate had climbed to 33.0 per 1,000, more than three times what the same week looked like in 2025. Epidemiologists partly attribute the rapid escalation to the immunity landscape left by the 2025–26 season, which lasted 16 weeks — more than three times the five-week duration of the 2024–25 season — but still ended before enough natural childhood infection could build broad population-level immunity heading into the current year. How the Surveillance Numbers Work When the KDCA reports an ILI rate, it is measuring the share of patients at designated sentinel clinics who present with the clinical definition of influenza-like illness: a sudden onset of fever at or above 38°C (100.4°F) accompanied by a cough or sore throat. That definition captures a broader set of respiratory pathogens than confirmed influenza alone — colds, RSV, and other viruses can produce the same presentation — but the ILI rate is used as the standard early-warning indicator because laboratory confirmation from every sentinel patient is impractical at scale. The virus detection rate — the share of sentinel patient specimens that actually test positive for influenza — provides the complementary picture. For Week 44 of 2026, the detection rate was 30.0%, more than double the 12.3% rate recorded when the season was first flagged in late August. When both metrics are rising together, as they have been throughout October, it confirms that actual influenza virus is driving the ILI increase rather than a confounding respiratory illness. Korea's sentinel network covers approximately 300 clinic-level institutions nationwide, though KDCA guidelines indicate the system was expanded to 800 participating clinics for the 2026–27 season. Hospitalization data come from a separate hospital-level component. The 461 hospitalizations recorded in Week 44 — roughly 2.6 times the same week in 2025 — came from that hospital network, as did the 21 confirmed flu-associated deaths. What Chungbuk Is Doing About It Chungbuk Province's campaign targets all children born between January 1, 2012, and August 31, 2026 — covering approximately 6 months through 14 years of age. The eligibility range reflects a nationwide policy change for the 2026–27 season: the KDCA expanded free childhood flu vaccination from the previous age ceiling of 13 years to include 14-year-olds, the first expansion of the age ceiling since the program's children's tier was last revised. During the November 9–December 8 intensive campaign window, the province has designated 341 sites: 14 public health centers (보건소) and 327 contracted private clinics (위탁의료기관). Parents who cannot locate a site can search the national Vaccination Assistant website (예방접종도우미) under "Find a Designated Medical Institution." Notably, children do not need to attend the clinic in their own registered district — any of the 341 sites will administer the vaccine, lowering the practical barrier for families who live near a clinic in an adjacent area. The vaccine administered is a trivalent influenza vaccine, one free dose per child. The trivalent formulation — covering three strains rather than the four covered by a quadrivalent shot — is the standard for the 2026–27 Korean national program, in line with the World Health Organization's recommendation for the Northern Hemisphere season. For this season, the H1N1 component targets a virus antigenically similar to A/Missouri/11/2025, the designated reference strain. The KDCA has confirmed that the vaccine shows high neutralization activity against the dominant circulating H1N1pdm09 strains detected in Korean surveillance. For families in which a parent or guardian cannot accompany the child, the province has a practical workaround: a guardian can prepare and sign a vaccination consent form and pre-screening questionnaire in advance, which the child brings to the clinic. Parents who want to streamline the visit can also complete the pre-screening electronically through the Vaccination Assistant portal before the appointment. After the intensive campaign window closes on December 8, free doses remain available through April 30, 2027. Oh Sang-sun, head of Chungbuk Province's Infectious Disease Management Division, described the rationale for the intensive format: "Influenza vaccination for children is the most effective tool for preventing the spread of infection in the community and protecting children's health during winter. We will work proactively during the intensive vaccination period to minimize gaps in coverage and to actively support more families in getting vaccinated." The Vaccination Coverage Gap The urgency behind Chungbuk's intensive campaign is easy to read in the national numbers. As of late October, roughly 40.5% of nationally eligible children had received flu shots — leaving nearly 60% of the eligible pediatric population unprotected as caseloads accelerate. That coverage level is well below the threshold generally required to interrupt transmission within dense school-age cohorts. Because H1N1pdm09 spreads efficiently in settings where children congregate — classrooms being the canonical transmission environment — a high attack rate among unvaccinated children is not simply a risk to those children individually; it drives community-level transmission that reaches infants, the elderly, and adults with underlying conditions who are at greatest risk of severe complications. The province's design decisions address several of the documented friction points in vaccination access: the no-district restriction means parents are not locked out if the nearest participating clinic happens to be across a ward boundary. The consent-form provision means older children do not need to wait for a parent to take half a day off work. The 341-site density means the median travel distance to a participating clinic is low for virtually any family in the province. National Context: Korea's Free Flu Program For the 2026–27 season, South Korea's national program covers three groups: children aged 6 months through 14 years, pregnant women, and adults aged 65 and older. The national children-and-pregnant-women phase launched September 21, with seniors phased in through mid-October. Children under 9 years old who have never been vaccinated, or who have received only one prior dose, require two doses at least four weeks apart. Children receiving a single dose for the season may choose from any of the 341 Chungbuk sites — or any participating site nationwide — without being restricted to their registered address. Who Is Most at Risk Influenza is clinically distinct from the common cold. While colds are caused by a range of viruses and typically produce upper-respiratory symptoms — runny nose, mild sore throat — influenza is characterized by sudden-onset high fever, chills, headache, and systemic muscle aches, with the fever threshold that defines ILI set at 38°C (100.4°F). The abrupt onset is one of its clinical signatures; most patients can identify the precise hour they began feeling ill. Children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those with underlying conditions such as cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, or compromised immunity face the highest risk of severe complications. The most common serious outcome is pneumonia — either from the influenza virus directly or from a secondary bacterial infection that takes hold after viral damage to the respiratory epithelium. The age-specific hospitalization patterns from KDCA surveillance show 65-and-older adults making up 60% of flu inpatients even as children lead in outpatient ILI rates, reflecting the characteristic bi-modal severity pattern of H1N1pdm09: high attack rates in children, high severity in elderly individuals. Annual vaccination is recommended even for those vaccinated in prior seasons. Circulating influenza strains evolve year over year through a process of antigenic drift — gradual mutation in the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface proteins that the immune system uses to recognize the virus. The annual update to the vaccine composition, coordinated by the WHO through its global surveillance network, is designed to track that drift. Vaccine-induced immunity also wanes over time, reinforcing the case for annual boosters. Vaccination should complement, not replace, standard hygiene measures: regular handwashing, mask use in crowded settings, and proper cough etiquette — covering the mouth and nose with a tissue or one's sleeve. Key Facts at a Glance Item Detail Campaign window November 9 – December 8, 2026 Extended free access Until April 30, 2027 Eligibility Born January 1, 2012 – August 31, 2026 (approx. 6 months–14 years) Vaccine Trivalent influenza vaccine, 1 dose, free Sites 341 (14 public health centers + 327 contracted clinics) Dominant virus Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 Week 44 ILI rate 22.8 per 1,000 outpatients (↑18.8% week-over-week) Week 44 ILI, ages 7–12 60.9 per 1,000 outpatients Week 44 hospitalizations 461 (≈2.6× same week 2025) Week 44 confirmed flu deaths 21 (vs. 4 same week 2025 — 5× increase) Virus detection rate (Wk 44) 30.0% Epidemic advisory issued September 11, 2026 National child vaccination uptake ~40.5% of eligible children (as of late October)

This illness is none other than Influenza A (H1N1), a strain of the seasonal flu which is seeing an uptick in its spread across various regions of the United States. GetCold Relief According to a report by Orlando's WFTV this past Sunday, the number of H1N1 cases is on the rise in central parts of the state. Health authorities are bracing for the potential simultaneous circulation of other respiratory viruses, such as COVID-19 and the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), in the coming weeks. Accurate and prompt diagnosis becomes crucial, especially for those at heightened risk of severe complications. CheckSymptoms Andrew Pekosz, an expert from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, noted that while antiviral medications are available for both influenza and COVID-19, their effectiveness hinges on timely administration. “Antivirals for COVID and the flu must be taken within the first few days of symptom onset to be effective,” Pekosz told WFTV. Understanding the Symptoms The flu typically manifests suddenly, with symptoms including fever, chills, muscle aches, cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, headaches, and intense fatigue. It's important to note that not everyone with the flu will experience a fever. GetCold Relief Conversely, symptoms of the common cold develop more slowly, whereas those of COVID-19 might appear anywhere from two to 14 days after exposure. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) cautions that symptom overlap makes it challenging to distinguish between these infections without diagnostic tests, which are essential for identifying the causative virus and guiding medical decisions. National Influenza Trends The rise in flu activity in Florida aligns with a nationwide trend. The CDC's recent surveillance report indicated that flu activity is climbing across many parts of the country, surpassing the levels usually seen at this time of year. During the epidemiological week ending October 31, U.S. public health labs identified 513 positive flu samples, with 502 being influenza A and 11 being influenza B. Among the 388 influenza A samples subtyped, 379 were A(H1N1)pdm09, making up 97.7% of the cases. This data represents results from participating U.S. labs and is not exclusive to Florida. GetCold Relief The CDC has reported that this virus has been seasonally circulating since 2009. While there are observed genetic changes among the circulating H1N1 viruses, it is still too early to assess their impact on vaccine efficacy this season. On Friday, they noted a 16.5% positivity rate for influenza A among tests conducted at their participating centers, with samples sequenced as the H1N1 subtype. Flu complications can be severe, leading to conditions like pneumonia, particularly in older adults over 65, young children, pregnant women, and individuals with certain chronic conditions. The CDC advises immediate medical attention for symptoms such as difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, confusion, or symptoms that improve and then return with increased severity. FindTreatments For those at greater risk of complications, antiviral treatments for the flu are most effective when started within the first two days of symptom onset. These medications require a doctor's prescription and may be recommended even after this period for certain patients. Health officials also advocate for annual flu vaccinations starting at six months of age, barring specific contraindications, as well as staying home when sick and avoiding close contact with vulnerable individuals. Last season, Florida experienced significant flu activity. In January, Southern Florida doctors warned of the strain on hospitals and emergency services from the H3N2 variant, known as subclade K. This previous outbreak involved a different subtype than the one currently prevalent in national records. Experts in Miami-Dade and Broward emphasized vaccination and early treatment to reduce hospitalization risks during that period. Flu activity began increasing in parts of the United States in late August and early September, earlier than in recent years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. While flu season typically starts in earnest around November, data used to track respiratory illnesses – like laboratory tests, hospitalizations and wastewater data – show that the season was already well underway before the clock struck Nov. 1. A new strain, a mutated version of H1N1, appears to be driving the spread, with some experts warning that it could play a hand in an earlier or longer season. Here's what that means for this winter's flu season and what experts say people should know. How many flu cases were reported nationwide? Flu cases began to take off in early fall this year, reaching an activity level in October not usually seen until December or January, according to wastewater data. "Seasonal flu activity continues to increase in many parts of the country and is higher than typically observed at this time of year," the CDC said on its influenza tracking site, FluView. The agency estimates 1.7 million illnesses, 25,000 hospitalizations and 1,400 deaths from flu so far this season as of Oct. 30. Two new pediatric deaths were also reported to the agency in the last week. As of Nov. 5, CDC projections found that flu infections were on the rise in 40 states and declining in none. The highest activity seems to be in Southern states and on the West Coast. Flu activity detected from wastewater was still categorized as "very low" nationwide as of Oct. 30, also according to the CDC. It noted that wastewater data tracking is experiencing a "brief gap" in updates due to a new contract with a testing company. It did not clarify how long this gap would last. Additional CDC data through Oct. 31 also showed that about 9.14% (4,694 ) of the 51,351 flu tests administered that week were reported positive to the National Respiratory and Enteric Virus Surveillance System. The vast majority of these confirmed illnesses (97%) were influenza A, the most common form of the flu. Wastewater data maintained by WasteWaterSCAN, a Stanford University-led tool for tracking the spread of disease, categorized flu activity as "high" nationally, meaning higher concentrations of the virus have been detected in the wastewater of more communities nationwide. The same data shows the earliest onset of flu in at least the last four years; samples positive for influenza A were at 71% in October, compared with 40% in September and just 20% in October 2025. The CDC likewise noted that seasonal flu activity began increasing around late August to early September Map of flu activity by state What are the new flu strains? The CDC said "it was too early to know what viruses may predominate" in late October, though scientists and health officials have signaled that they are paying extra attention to a few strains. This doesn't mean this year's viruses have transformed into something dramatically more dangerous or deadly. Rather, mutations have likely made them a little better at slipping past immunity people build from previous infections and vaccines. H1N1, a type of influenza A, is the primary diagnosis behind this year's flu season thus far. You may recognize the name from the "swine flu" pandemic of 2009, caused by a novel strain called H1N1/09. Health officials noted that this year's virus remains part of the long-circulating seasonal H1N1 lineage rather than a new pandemic strain. The most common H1N1 strain currently is the genetic subgroup known as subclade D.3.1.1. Scientists are watching the strain because it has accumulated additional mutations in parts of the virus targeted by human antibodies, raising concerns that some newer versions may be building upon mutations and drifting away from existing immunity almost "in real time," according to a recent study. The study was published on the preprint server bioRxiv, meaning the research has not yet completed the peer-review process. "Why we think we're seeing this now, nobody really knows, but likely it's due to mutations," Dr. Corey K. Smith, emergency physician and Regional Medical Director at Teladoc Health, told USA TODAY. "And what happens is we were all exposed to H1N1 back in 2009, and after some time, as it mutates - and even though we developed this shield, this armor - we have slightly decreased immunity to it." Notably, early evidence shows D.3.1.1 may impact groups of people differently. Some people's antibodies appear to still "recognize" the strain pretty well, while others seem to lose protection. In the September study, researchers noted that teenagers and younger adults seemed to be more affected than adults, specifically people between 15 and 25. This may be thanks to something called "immune imprinting" - a phenomenon in which the body "remembers" the first time it encountered a pathogen and shapes every reaction for the rest of your life based at least partially on this first encounter. So, the first flu strain you were exposed to as a child is the basis for how your immune system responds now. This is why we may see some strains of common illness impacting groups differently along generational lines. In this specific case, the researchers believe that people who were likely first exposed to H1N1 during or shortly after the 2009 pandemic were more affected by D.3.1.1 than people who caught the older strain of H1N1 before 2009. "This is pretty much how viruses work. These viruses, they sit back and say, 'hey, let's attack people, let's attack animals, let's attack birds,' whatever," said Smith. "But as they encounter us and our antibodies, they kind of go back to their homes and say, 'Hey, let's mutate and see if we can come back bigger and stronger next year or next season'." The doctors and scientists who formulate next year's flu shot review these patterns and try to make predictions on how to prevent the next wave, he continued. What are the latest flu symptoms? Symptoms associated with D.3.1.1 are the same as other influenza viruses and include: Fever Body aches and chills Cough Runny or stuffy nose and sneezing Sore throat Headache Fatigue Smith noted that patients often wonder which signs or symptoms can help them figure out whether they have the flu or another respiratory illness, like COVID. One major distinction he noted is the presence or absence of fever and the sniffles. "The symptoms initially start as being relatively similar as you cross different viruses: cough, congestion, malaise (feeling generally unwell), weakness, body aches and a fever," meaning a temperature of 100.4 or higher, he said. Fever, especially in adults, is a strong indicator of flu, along with the sudden onset of body aches and chills. If you felt fine earlier and suddenly "feel like you got hit by a Mack truck" an hour or two later, it is more likely the flu, he explained. "With a common cold, you may have a cough and a runny nose, but you don't have those extreme body aches and head pain," Smith also said. "With COVID, you can have a fever or a little cough, but congestion tends to be the main thing, plus or minus headache and anosmia (loss of taste and smell)." How to protect yourself from the flu. You may be tired of hearing it, but the old cliché is true: Washing your hands well – and often – is one of the best ways to keep contagious illnesses at bay, according to the CDC. This applies to all the ailments above and others that often circulate during the wintertime, like respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV. Health agencies recommend washing your hands with hot, soapy water for at least 20 seconds. It's also important to wash them before and after eating, before and after handling food, after using the bathroom and after being around sick people or touching surfaces that could be contaminated. Mask-wearing while sick or out and about during illness season can also help prevent the spread. This is especially important for people at risk of more serious disease, including children and older adults, pregnant people, immunocompromised people and those with underlying conditions like obesity and diabetes. The most effective way to prevent serious illness from the flu is vaccination, according to the World Health Organization, CDC and other prominent medical institutions. Earlier this year, leading medical groups came together to release vaccine recommendations as federal agencies continue to share inconsistent information amid a guideline shakeup and legal challenges under the leadership of known vaccine skeptic and health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The guide recommends the yearly influenza shot to everyone aged six months or older (including pregnant people), with a few exceptions for people with certain medical conditions. People 65+ should recieve a higher dose, if possible. Even if it doesn't stop you from catching the flu entirely, vaccination has still been shown to reduce the severity and length of illness. "That's what vaccines do. It creates a stronger immune response and bigger, stronger antibodies. It gives us a little preview, like a film, like a trailer of what's about to come," said Smith. "Please, get vaccinated. It's not too late and it does contain various mutations and strains of the H1N1, including those that are circulating this year." Featured Weekly Ad
